title: Smile and Choir
premise: Wren Lockridge has spent years at Hollowmere Hospice perfecting the art of being unnoticed, because she learned young that attention is how things find you. When the mirrors begin lagging a second behind reality, she uncovers the hospice's founding secret: the building is a seal, and the dying who count backwards are not fading—they are feeding something that keeps worse things out. The founders' ritual was never finished; it requires a living keeper to walk it through on the night of the lag, and every previous keeper chose survival over duty. Wren must decide whether to complete the ritual—which demands she surrender her memories of everyone she has ever loved—or let the seal fail and unleash what waits behind the one-second delay. She finishes it, but the final price is that she remembers only that she loved someone, never who—until the last page, when a familiar voice begins counting backwards beside her.
about_author: Lior Delacroix is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who writes horror about institutions, rituals, and the quiet bargains people make to keep going. They live in a coastal town where they claim the fog arrives exactly on schedule.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Introduces Hollowmere Hospice and Wren's compulsive rituals: lights checked, doors counted, invisibility maintained. A dying patient, Mr. Aldous, counts backwards from thirty in his sleep—and stops at zero with a smile. Emotional beat: eerie unease beneath Wren's careful control.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She notices her reflection in the staff bathroom mirror lags—a blink arriving after her own. She tests it with a dropped cup; the reflection drops it late. Emotional beat: the vertigo of realizing her defenses were always aimed at something real.

chapters.title: Doors I Have Counted
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, with flashbacks to childhood, when her grandmother taught her to stay unseen 'so they can't pick you.' We learn Wren's sister vanished years ago after being 'noticed.' Emotional beat: grief reframed as superstition.

chapters.title: The Founder's Ledger
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the sealed basement archive she finds the 1911 ledger of founder Edith Marlowe: patient names, death dates, and backwards counts—all ending at zero on the same calendar night. Emotional beat: dread hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: What the Dying Know
chapters.summary: Alternating Wren and Mr. Aldous POV. Aldous, lucid for one hour, tells her the counting isn't dying—it's answering a call. He begs her not to finish what the founders started, then forgets he spoke. Emotional beat: compassion tangled with warning.

chapters.title: The New Nurse
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A replacement nurse, Callum Reyes, arrives—warm, observant, impossible to ignore. Wren's invisibility tactics fail around him, and the mirrors worsen wherever he stands. Emotional beat: reluctant attraction against self-preservation.

chapters.title: Lag
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. He admits he requested this posting; his mother died at Hollowmere counting backwards, and he needs to know why. The hallway mirror shows them both standing there a full second before they arrive. Emotional beat: two lonely people choosing each other over caution.

chapters.title: Edith Marlowe's Confession
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Hidden pages of the ledger reveal the ritual: the seal was left unfinished when the last keeper fled in 1938. It requires a willing keeper to walk seven stations on the night of deepest lag, giving up 'what holds her to the world.' Emotional beat: the weight of an inherited debt.

chapters.title: Zero Night Approaching
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Patients across the ward begin counting in unison during the same minute each night. The administrator dismisses it; Wren maps the counts against the ledger and finds the convergence date: six days away. Emotional beat: ticking-clock urgency.

chapters.title: The Thing Behind the Glass
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. Alone at night, Callum watches his reflection move independently—smiling when he doesn't. It mouths words: SHE REMEMBERS US. He tells Wren; she recognizes the phrase from her grandmother. Emotional beat: terror made intimate.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Box
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Visiting her childhood home, Wren finds her grandmother's box: photographs of Hollowmere, a keeper's iron key, and a note—'Your sister was taken because I broke the count. Finish it or lose another.' Emotional beat: family guilt as inheritance.

chapters.title: Seven Stations
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She deciphers the ritual's stations: the well, the chapel bell, the birthing room, the morgue slab, the mirror hall, the founder's grave, and the threshold door. Each demands a memory as payment. Emotional beat: grim inventory of what she'll lose.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Wren and Callum grow close despite everything; he offers to walk the ritual instead. Wren refuses—the ledger says the keeper must be 'one who hears.' Their first kiss happens while the whole ward counts backwards. Emotional beat: tenderness sharpened by doom.

chapters.title: The First Station: The Well
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Two nights early, testing the ritual, Wren descends to the dry well. Her reflection appears at the bottom before she does. She pays a small memory—her tenth birthday—and climbs out unable to recall why she once feared the dark. Emotional beat: the horror of voluntary loss.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. Callum researches the 1938 keeper, Ada Voss, and finds she survived by fleeing—and that Ada Voss is Wren's great-aunt, meaning the debt runs in Wren's blood. He hesitates to tell her. Emotional beat: love tested by secrets.

chapters.title: The Mirror Hall
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The hospice's long mirror corridor now lags three seconds, and reflections have begun moving toward the glass from the other side. Wren sees her missing sister among them, mouthing her name. Emotional beat: hope weaponized as a trap.

chapters.title: Ada Voss Returns
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. An old woman arrives at the hospice as a patient: Ada Voss, the fleeing keeper, come back to die where she failed. She confesses the ritual's true cost and warns that the thing behind the glass will offer Wren exactly what she most wants. Emotional beat: mercy and menace in one voice.

chapters.title: Zero Night
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The convergence begins: every patient counts aloud, mirrors go dark then clear, and the building exhales. Wren starts the stations while Callum holds the wards' doors counted shut. Emotional beat: resolve under siege.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At the fifth station, the thing behind the glass wears her sister's face and offers to give her back—if Wren abandons the ritual. Wren sees through it only because the offer includes memories she'd already paid away. Emotional beat: heartbreak as armor.

chapters.title: The Threshold Door
chapters.summary: Climax. Wren's POV. At the final station she must surrender 'what holds her to the world': her love itself. Callum reaches her and begs her to stop; instead she asks him to remember for both of them. She speaks the closing words as the seal completes and the mirrors shatter inward. Emotional beat: sacrifice transfigured into devotion.

chapters.title: After the Counting
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. The hospice is quiet; patients die peacefully, counting forward now. Wren wakes calm and hollow, knowing she loved someone but not who. Callum stays, keeping her company without explaining, honoring her request. Emotional beat: grief without its object.

chapters.title: Smile and Choir
chapters.summary: Final chapter, dual POV. Months later, Wren tends the dying again, invisible by choice rather than fear. One night a new patient smiles and begins counting backwards—from ten—and Wren feels something stir that memory cannot name. Callum takes her hand. Emotional beat: bittersweet grace; love outlasting its record.
